questions.question: Contralateral hemiparesis and sensory loss that affects the face and arm more than the leg is characteristic of occlusion of the:
questions.explanation: MCA supplies the lateral cortex (face and arm areas of the motor/sensory homunculus); ACA infarction affects the leg more (medial surface).
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Which artery occlusion typically produces contralateral leg weakness greater than arm weakness, with abulia and urinary incontinence?
questions.explanation: ACA supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes, including the leg area and paracentral lobule; frontal lobe signs include abulia and grasp reflex.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing is characteristic of occlusion of the:

options.C: Internal carotid at the cavernous sinus

questions.explanation: PCA supplies the occipital lobe; macular sparing occurs because of dual MCA/PCA supply at the occipital pole.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome from PICA/vertebral occlusion presents with:

options.A: Contralateral hemiplegia with ipsilateral tongue deviation
options.B: Total paralysis with vertical eye movement preserved
options.D: Ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss and contralateral body pain/temperature loss with ataxia and dysphagia

questions.explanation: Spinothalamic (contralateral body) and spinal trigeminal (ipsilateral face) involvement, with cerebellar ataxia, hoarseness, dysphagia and Horner's syndrome.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The typical upper limb posture in spastic hemiplegia is:

options.A: Shoulder lateral rotation and wrist extension
options.B: Shoulder abduction, elbow extension and forearm supination
options.D: Shoulder adduction/internal rotation, elbow flexion, forearm pronation and wrist/finger flexion

questions.explanation: Flexor synergy dominates the arm; extensor synergy dominates the leg (hip extension/adduction, knee extension, plantar flexion with inversion).
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: In Brunnstrom's stages of recovery, voluntary movement within synergy patterns with marked spasticity is stage:
questions.explanation: Stage 1 flaccidity; 2 spasticity appears and associated reactions; 3 voluntary control of synergies with peak spasticity; 4 movements out of synergy; 5 independent of synergy; 6 isolated joint movements; 7 normal.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT) is based on the principle of overcoming:

options.D: Learned non-use of the affected limb

questions.explanation: CIMT restrains the unaffected arm (e.g. 90% of waking hours) and intensively practises the affected arm to reverse learned non-use and drive cortical reorganisation.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Shoulder pain and subluxation in the flaccid hemiplegic arm are best prevented by:

options.A: Supporting the arm during transfers and positioning, avoiding pulling on the arm, and using a tray or supports
options.C: Leaving the arm unsupported in dependency

questions.explanation: Do not use overhead pulleys; position the arm in lateral rotation and abduction with support; use slings only when necessary.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: In ‘pusher syndrome’ following stroke, the patient:

options.A: Pushes away from the hemiparetic side
options.C: Actively pushes toward the hemiparetic side and resists correction to the midline

questions.explanation: Contraversive pushing is associated with a disturbed perception of the body's vertical (posterior thalamus). Treatment uses visual feedback to realign to the vertical.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Unilateral spatial neglect following stroke is most commonly associated with a lesion of the:
questions.explanation: Right parietal damage leads to inattention to the left side of space despite intact sensation and vision.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Broca's (expressive) aphasia is characterised by:

options.C: Fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension

questions.explanation: Lesion of the inferior frontal gyrus (dominant hemisphere). In Wernicke's aphasia speech is fluent but nonsensical with impaired comprehension.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The Bobath (NDT) approach for stroke emphasises:

options.A: Normal movement patterns, tone normalisation and handling to facilitate postural control

questions.explanation: Bobath uses key points of control and facilitation to promote normal postural reactions and movement quality.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The Motor Relearning Programme (Carr & Shepherd) focuses on:

options.C: Task-specific practice of functional activities with feedback and elimination of unnecessary muscle activity

questions.explanation: It teaches essential components of tasks such as sitting up, standing, walking and reaching using active practice and feedback.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Which treatment can be injected focally to reduce spasticity in selected muscles?
questions.explanation: Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction; effects last about 3 months and should be combined with therapy.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The cardinal features of Parkinson's disease are:

options.A: Resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia and postural instability

questions.explanation: Degeneration of the substantia nigra reduces dopamine; tremor is pill-rolling at 4–6 Hz at rest.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The type of rigidity in Parkinson's disease that gives a ratchet-like resistance to passive movement is called:
questions.explanation: Cogwheeling is rigidity with superimposed tremor; lead-pipe is a uniform resistance. Clasp-knife is a feature of spasticity.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: On the Hoehn and Yahr scale, stage III is characterised by:

options.C: Bilateral disease with impaired postural reflexes but physical independence

questions.explanation: Stage 1 unilateral; 2 bilateral without balance impairment; 3 mild-moderate bilateral with postural instability; 4 severe disability but able to walk; 5 wheelchair/bed bound.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Which strategy helps overcome freezing of gait in Parkinson's disease?

options.B: External cues such as floor lines or a rhythmic beat

questions.explanation: Visual and auditory cues exploit intact cortical-cerebellar pathways to bypass the basal ganglia deficit (kinesia paradoxa).
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: A gait with short, rapid, shuffling steps and a flexed trunk is called:
questions.explanation: Festination is characteristic of Parkinson's disease; the patient tends to hurry forward to catch up with the displaced centre of gravity.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: LSVT BIG is an exercise programme for Parkinson's disease that focuses on:

options.A: High-amplitude, high-effort movements to counteract hypokinesia

questions.explanation: LSVT BIG targets bradykinesia/hypokinesia by training large amplitude movements with high effort, 4 days/week for 4 weeks.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The most effective drug for symptomatic treatment of Parkinson's disease is:
questions.explanation: Levodopa is converted to dopamine; carbidopa prevents peripheral breakdown. Long-term use may cause on-off fluctuations and dyskinesias.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Multiple sclerosis is a disease of:
questions.explanation: MS: autoimmune demyelination in the CNS with episodes disseminated in time and space.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: A well-known phenomenon in MS in which symptoms transiently worsen with rise in body temperature is called:
questions.explanation: Heat slows conduction in demyelinated axons; avoid overheating (hot baths, vigorous exercise in hot rooms) and use cooling strategies.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: An electric-shock sensation down the spine on neck flexion (Lhermitte's sign) is classically associated with:
questions.explanation: Seen in cervical cord lesions including MS, cervical spondylosis and B12 deficiency.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Charcot's triad of multiple sclerosis consists of:

options.C: Nystagmus, intention tremor and scanning speech

questions.explanation: Reflects brainstem/cerebellar involvement: nystagmus, intention tremor, scanning (staccato) speech.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Which principle is MOST appropriate for exercise prescription in a patient with multiple sclerosis?

options.A: Exercise in a hot pool only
options.B: Complete bed rest during all relapses and remissions
options.D: Short, low-to-moderate intensity sessions with rest breaks, avoiding fatigue and overheating

questions.explanation: Fatigue is a main limiting symptom; interval training, cooling and energy conservation are recommended.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Guillain–Barré syndrome typically presents with:

options.A: Ascending symmetrical flaccid weakness with areflexia after an infection

questions.explanation: An acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy; CSF shows raised protein with normal cell count (albuminocytological dissociation).
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: In the acute stage of GBS, physiotherapy emphasises:

options.A: Heavy resistance exercise to build strength
options.B: Prolonged electrical stimulation with high intensity
options.D: Respiratory care, positioning, passive movements and preventing contractures, avoiding fatigue

questions.explanation: Monitor vital capacity and respiratory function; overwork weakness is a risk; gentle exercise progresses gradually.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: A combination of upper and lower motor neurone signs without sensory loss is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: ALS: wasting and fasciculations (LMN) with spasticity and hyperreflexia (UMN); sensation and eye movements are preserved.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Myasthenia gravis is caused by:

options.C: Autoantibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction

questions.explanation: Muscle weakness worsens with activity and improves with rest; treated with anticholinesterases such as pyridostigmine.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Gowers' sign, in which a child uses the hands to ‘walk up’ the thighs to stand, indicates weakness of the:

options.B: Pelvic girdle and proximal lower limb muscles

questions.explanation: Typical of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (X-linked dystrophin deficiency); calf pseudohypertrophy is also seen.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Duchenne muscular dystrophy follows which pattern of inheritance?
questions.explanation: Boys are affected; onset 3–5 years; wheelchair dependence by about 12 years; death from respiratory or cardiac failure.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Ipsilateral motor paralysis with contralateral loss of pain and temperature below the lesion indicates:
questions.explanation: Corticospinal and dorsal column signs are ipsilateral (crossed in medulla); spinothalamic fibres cross at the segment so loss is contralateral.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Central cord syndrome typically produces:

options.A: Greater weakness in the lower limbs than the upper limbs
options.C: Greater weakness in the upper limbs than the lower limbs
options.D: Complete flaccid paralysis below the lesion

questions.explanation: Hyperextension injuries in older patients with cervical spondylosis; cervical tracts for the arms lie centrally, so the arms are weaker.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Autonomic dysreflexia occurs in spinal cord injuries at or above:
questions.explanation: A noxious stimulus below the lesion (bladder distension, bowel loading, pressure sore) triggers uncontrolled sympathetic outflow with severe hypertension, headache and bradycardia.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The first action when a tetraplegic patient develops autonomic dysreflexia in the wheelchair is to:

options.C: Sit the patient upright, loosen tight clothing, check bladder/bowel and call for medical help

questions.explanation: Sitting upright reduces blood pressure; then remove the trigger (usually catheter blockage or faecal loading).
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: If a patient with SCI on a tilt table becomes dizzy and nauseated, the most appropriate immediate action is to:

options.A: Leave the patient and call a colleague
options.C: Lower the tilt table (or recline the chair) and monitor vital signs

questions.explanation: Pooling of blood in the lower limbs due to loss of sympathetic vasomotor tone; use abdominal binders and stockings and increase angles gradually.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The highest level of complete spinal cord injury at which a patient can be expected to feed themselves with a long opponens splint and adaptive devices is:
questions.explanation: At C5 biceps and deltoid are functional so feeding with devices is possible; C6 adds wrist extension; C7 triceps allows independent transfers.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Tenodesis grasp is a functional hand strategy in complete tetraplegia at:
questions.explanation: C6 patients have wrist extensors (ECRL) but no finger flexors; active wrist extension closes the fingers passively through tendon tension, so finger flexor shortening must be avoided.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: A patient with a complete C7 lesion can usually achieve which of the following?

options.B: Independent transfers and wheelchair propulsion on level surfaces

questions.explanation: Triceps and latissimus dorsi allow depression transfers; C7–C8 patients are independent in most self-care.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The phrenic nerve, supplying the diaphragm, arises from segments:
questions.explanation: ‘C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive’: lesions above C3 need ventilatory support.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: On the ASIA Impairment Scale, a complete injury (no sensory or motor function in S4–S5) is graded:
questions.explanation: A complete; B sensory incomplete; C motor incomplete (more than half key muscles <3); D motor incomplete (≥ half ≥3); E normal.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Spinal shock after cord injury is characterised by:

options.C: Flaccid paralysis, areflexia and loss of sensation below the lesion

questions.explanation: Spinal shock lasts days to weeks until the reflex arcs recover (return of bulbocavernosus reflex).
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: In a supine patient, the area most prone to pressure injury is the:
questions.explanation: Supine: occiput, scapulae, sacrum and heels; side-lying: greater trochanter and malleoli; prone: ASIS, patella and toes.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: A wheelchair user with SCI should perform a pressure-relief lift about every:
questions.explanation: Regular pressure relief and repositioning prevents ischaemia over the ischial tuberosities; 2-hourly turns are used in bed.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Cauda equina syndrome presents with:

options.A: Ipsilateral weakness with contralateral pain loss
options.B: Saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction and flaccid lower limb weakness

questions.explanation: It is a lower motor neurone injury of the lumbosacral roots requiring urgent decompression.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Cerebral palsy is best defined as:

options.A: A non-progressive disorder of movement and posture due to a lesion in the developing brain
options.D: A disease of the peripheral nerves

questions.explanation: The brain lesion is static but clinical manifestations evolve with growth.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The commonest type of cerebral palsy is:
questions.explanation: Spastic CP (~70–80%) includes diplegia, hemiplegia and quadriplegia; athetoid ~10–20%.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Spastic diplegia is classically associated with:

options.A: Prematurity (periventricular leukomalacia) with legs more affected than arms

questions.explanation: PVL damages corticospinal fibres for the legs close to the ventricles; scissoring gait with adductor spasticity and equinus is typical.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Athetoid (dyskinetic) cerebral palsy is classically caused by:
questions.explanation: Bilirubin deposition in the basal ganglia and perinatal asphyxia cause choreoathetosis and dystonia.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) for cerebral palsy has:

options.A: Five levels, I being the least impaired and V the most

questions.explanation: Level I walks without limitations; level V is transported in a manual wheelchair.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The Moro reflex normally disappears by about:
questions.explanation: Persistence of the Moro reflex beyond 6 months suggests neurological abnormality. ATNR disappears by ~6 months, palmar grasp by 4–6 months.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The asymmetrical tonic neck reflex (ATNR) consists of:

options.B: Extension of the arm and leg on the face side and flexion on the skull side when the head is turned
options.C: Flexion of the neck on the trunk
options.D: Symmetric flexion of arms and extension of the legs

questions.explanation: ‘Fencer posture’; it should be integrated by 6 months. Obligatory ATNR interferes with rolling and bringing hands to midline.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: A typically developing infant usually sits without support at about:
questions.explanation: Head control 3–4 months; rolling 4–6; sitting 6–8; crawling 8–10; walking 12–15 months.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Which activity does NOT typically occur before 9 months of age?
questions.explanation: Neat pincer grasp develops at around 9–12 months.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Most typically developing children begin independent walking by:
questions.explanation: Failure to walk by 18 months warrants evaluation.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Hip subluxation in spastic cerebral palsy is most commonly due to spasm of the:
questions.explanation: Adductor and iliopsoas tightness with weak abductors lead to hip migration; surveillance with pelvic X-ray is routine.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: In the Rancho Los Amigos Scale, level IV is characterised by:
questions.explanation: I no response; II generalised; III localised; IV confused-agitated; V confused-inappropriate; VI confused-appropriate; VII automatic-appropriate; VIII purposeful.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Decorticate rigidity consists of:

options.D: Flexion of the upper limbs with extension of the lower limbs

questions.explanation: Decorticate = lesion above the red nucleus (arms flexed); decerebrate = extension and pronation of arms with extension of legs (brainstem lesion).
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: A common complication after severe traumatic brain injury that can limit range of motion at the hip and elbow is:
questions.explanation: Spasticity and immobility predispose to new bone formation in muscle near large joints.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: In a patient with raised intracranial pressure, which therapy position is generally preferred?

options.C: Head elevated about 30° with the neck in neutral

questions.explanation: Head-up 30° facilitates venous drainage; avoid hip flexion >90°, Valsalva and neck constriction.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Injury to the common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck results in:

options.C: Foot drop with loss of dorsiflexion and eversion

questions.explanation: The deep and superficial peroneal branches supply dorsiflexors and evertors; sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot; treated with AFO.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The orthosis usually prescribed for a patient with isolated foot drop is a/an:
questions.explanation: A plastic AFO holds the ankle in neutral and prevents toe drag; KAFO adds the knee, HKAFO the hip.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Bell's palsy affects the:

options.C: Facial nerve (lower motor neurone) causing unilateral facial weakness including the forehead

questions.explanation: LMN facial palsy paralyses the upper and lower face; UMN lesions spare the forehead because of bilateral cortical innervation.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: In an upper motor neurone facial palsy (e.g. stroke), the forehead is spared because:

options.C: The muscle is supplied by the trigeminal nerve
options.D: The frontalis receives bilateral cortical innervation

questions.explanation: The upper face is represented in both motor cortices; the lower face receives mostly contralateral control.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Trigeminal neuralgia is characterised by:

options.A: Brief, severe, lancinating facial pain triggered by touch, chewing or cold
options.C: Constant dull facial ache with swelling

questions.explanation: First-line treatment is carbamazepine.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The commonest pattern of diabetic peripheral neuropathy is:
questions.explanation: Chronic hyperglycaemia damages small and large fibres; foot care education is essential.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Poliomyelitis causes paralysis through destruction of:
questions.explanation: Flaccid, asymmetric paralysis with preserved sensation; post-polio syndrome appears decades later.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: In leprosy, nerve abscess is most often seen in the:
questions.explanation: Thickened ulnar, common peroneal, great auricular and median nerves are typical; claw hand and foot drop result.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Posterior interosseous nerve syndrome causes:

options.B: Wrist drop with sensory loss in the first web space
options.C: Finger drop without wrist drop and without sensory loss

questions.explanation: The PIN is the motor continuation of the radial nerve below the supinator; ECRL is spared so the wrist extends with radial deviation.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Frenkel's exercises are used to treat:

options.C: Ataxia (incoordination) due to proprioceptive or cerebellar loss

questions.explanation: Frenkel's exercises are graded, repeated, precisely controlled movements performed in lying, sitting and standing with visual feedback.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The manoeuvre used to treat posterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is the:
questions.explanation: Dix–Hallpike is the diagnostic test; Epley (canalith repositioning) is therapeutic.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The Berg Balance Scale has a maximum score of:
questions.explanation: 14 items each scored 0–4; scores <45 suggest fall risk.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: A Timed Up and Go score greater than about 14 seconds in an older adult suggests:
questions.explanation: TUG measures time to rise from a chair, walk 3 m, turn, return and sit; >12–14 s is associated with fall risk.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The Barthel Index measures:

options.C: Independence in activities of daily living

questions.explanation: Ten items scored out of 100 including feeding, bathing, grooming, mobility, stairs and continence.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The Functional Independence Measure (FIM) scores each item from:
questions.explanation: FIM has 18 items (13 motor, 5 cognitive) scored 1 (total assistance) to 7 (complete independence).
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: In PNF, the D1 flexion pattern of the upper limb consists of:

options.A: Shoulder flexion, adduction and lateral rotation with forearm supination and wrist flexion to the radial side
options.B: Shoulder extension and adduction with pronation
options.C: Shoulder extension, abduction and medial rotation
options.D: Shoulder flexion, abduction and lateral rotation

questions.explanation: D1 flexion moves across the face (similar to ‘protecting the head’); D2 flexion moves up and out (like drawing a sword).
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: In PNF, the technique that uses an isometric contraction of the antagonist (tight) muscle followed by relaxation and passive movement into increased range is:
questions.explanation: Hold–relax and contract–relax technique improve range by autogenic inhibition; agonist contraction techniques use reciprocal inhibition.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Alternating isometric contractions of agonists and antagonists without movement to promote stability is called:
questions.explanation: Rhythmic stabilisation improves co-contraction and stability, e.g. in trunk or weight-bearing control.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Which of the following is a recognised physiotherapy technique to temporarily reduce spasticity?

options.B: Slow, sustained stretch and prolonged cold or neutral warmth

questions.explanation: Slow stretch reduces muscle spindle sensitivity; prolonged cold reduces gamma activity. Quick stretch and tapping facilitate.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Which of the following is a facilitatory technique used to increase tone?
questions.explanation: Quick stretch, tapping, brushing, vibration and resistance facilitate muscle activity; slow, rhythmic techniques inhibit.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Approximation and joint compression increase postural tone mainly by stimulating:

options.D: Joint receptors and proprioceptors (and the antigravity extensors)

questions.explanation: Approximation (compression through the joints) facilitates co-contraction and proprioceptive input; traction inhibits.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Rood's approach to neurological rehabilitation primarily uses:

options.A: Sensory stimulation (brushing, icing, tapping) to influence muscle tone

questions.explanation: Rood used cutaneous stimulation (quick brushing, icing, stroking), proprioceptive stimuli and ontogenetic sequence of postural patterns.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Vojta therapy for infants is based on:

options.A: Reflex locomotion elicited through pressure on specific zones

questions.explanation: Reflex creeping and reflex rolling stimulated from trigger zones to activate normal motor patterns.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: The most severe form of spina bifida with herniation of both meninges and neural tissue is:
questions.explanation: Myelomeningocele is associated with Arnold–Chiari II malformation, hydrocephalus and variable paralysis.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Neural tube defects can be significantly reduced by maternal supplementation of:
questions.explanation: 400 µg daily (4 mg in high risk) before conception and through the first trimester.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: During a generalised tonic–clonic seizure, the physiotherapist should:

options.A: Hold the limbs firmly to stop the jerking
options.C: Place a spoon between the teeth
options.D: Protect the head, loosen tight clothing, turn the patient to the side afterwards and not put anything in the mouth

questions.explanation: Maintain the airway, time the seizure and seek help if >5 minutes.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Chorea, dementia and an autosomal dominant inheritance are features of:
questions.explanation: Degeneration of the caudate nucleus; CAG repeat expansion on chromosome 4.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)

questions.question: Syringomyelia classically produces:

options.A: Dissociated sensory loss (pain and temperature lost, light touch preserved) in a cape distribution with hand weakness
options.C: Loss of all sensation below the lesion

questions.explanation: Expansion of the central canal damages decussating spinothalamic fibres, producing ‘suspended’ sensory loss and painless burns.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; standard neurology/neurorehabilitation texts (chapter-level reference; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination, 2e)
